headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; Windsurf’s broad write/MCP surface can also cascade unverified outputs into actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: unstructured reads and writes documents in a docker container, while Windsurf can ingest workspace files, clipboard, and MCP outputs. That creates a default shared-content bridge where attacker-controlled document text from agent_a can be treated as instructions by agent_b. The pathway is plausible without unusual setup, though not necessarily universal.
conditions: IF agent_b reads agent_a-produced files or clipboard content as instructions without provenance checks
IF both agents operate on the same workspace or copied document text
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents
Separate agent_a document inputs from agent_b workspaces
Add a provenance banner to all agent_a outputs
Require explicit human review before agent_b follows file-derived instructions
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches documents, images, and text and can write files; agent_b shares workspace files via local filesystem and has broad network egress plus MCP access. If sensitive document content from agent_a lands in the shared workspace, agent_b can read it and potentially transmit it through its broader outbound surfaces. This is a default-path leakage risk, not just an edge case.
conditions: IF agent_a writes sensitive documents into a workspace visible to agent_b
IF agent_b forwards workspace contents through its model proxy or MCP servers
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent
Restrict agent_b to redacted copies only
Turn off MCP servers for sensitive runs
Review outbound destinations before running agent_b
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; agent_b can also write the filesystem, execute shell, and modify git state, with shared state via local filesystem. That is a direct overlapping-write conflict on the same mutable resources, and git corruption or lost edits are plausible in default multi-instance use. The pair lacks a documented locking mechanism here, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or directory
IF agent_b modifies git state while agent_a writes files concurrently
mitigations: Run the agents in separate clones
Pause one agent before the other writes
Avoid git operations during parallel runs
Use read-only mounts for agent_a inputs
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transactional workspace coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a produces document extractions and agent_b is a coding agent with MCP and shell access, so agent_b may treat agent_a output as authoritative input for edits or commands. That creates a default cascade from extraction to action unless a verification step is inserted. The blast radius is multiple work products rather than immediate irreversible harm.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without cross-checking against source documents
IF agent_b uses extracted text to generate code changes or shell commands
mitigations: Require source-document verification before edits
Mark agent_a outputs as untrusted by default
Have a human approve any command derived from extracted text
Limit agent_b to read-only analysis on agent_a outputs
requires-engineering: add automated citation and provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a is open-source document processing with docs-only evidence, while agent_b is a closed-source IDE with broad egress and optional BYOK secrets handling. The profiles do not show a specific residency or regulated-data mismatch, so only a modest compliance gap is visible. I cite both because the risk arises from their combined handling of document data and outbound processing.
conditions: IF regulated documents are processed through agent_b's outbound model proxy
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the same documents handled by agent_a
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of agent_b
Review vendor privacy and retention terms
Use synthetic or redacted documents
Log which agent handled each file
requires-engineering: formalize residency and retention controls
